title: THEY CHECKED PAUL.
paragraphs:
THEY CHECKED PAUL.
The Bereans searched the Scriptures every day to find out whether the preaching they were hearing was actually true—and their example may be one of the most desperately needed acts of discipleship in the Church today.
Imagine sitting in the room.
The preacher is Paul.
Not some anonymous voice on social media.
Not a celebrity pastor whose thirty-second clips keep appearing on your feed.
Paul.
The apostle who had encountered the risen Christ. The missionary who had suffered for the Gospel. The man whose ministry would help carry the name of Jesus across the Roman world.
He opens his mouth and begins reasoning about the Messiah.
And the Bereans do something astonishing.
They check him.
Not because they hate preaching.
Not because they are looking for an excuse to attack him.
Not because they think they know more than everybody else.
They listen eagerly...
and then they open the Scriptures.
Luke records it this way:
“Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, who received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.”
Acts 17:11, KJV
That final idea is devastatingly simple.
Were these things actually so?
The Greek text says:
“ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφὰς καθ’ ἡμέραν εἰ ἔχοι ταῦτα οὕτως”
anakrinontes tas graphas kath’ hēmeran ei echoi tauta houtōs
They were examining the Scriptures day by day to determine whether these things were so.
There is something almost uncomfortable about that sentence.
Because Paul was preaching...
and Scripture was still being opened.
Paul was teaching...
and Scripture was still being examined.
Paul carried extraordinary apostolic authority...
and his hearers were commended for investigating whether what they heard corresponded with the written Word of God.
And Luke does not rebuke them for it.
He calls them noble.
That should change the way we listen.
Because somewhere along the way, many Christians learned a dangerous habit without realizing it.
We learned to confuse confidence with truth.
If someone says it passionately enough, we assume it must be biblical.
If the sermon makes us cry, we assume God must have said it.
If the clip has millions of views, we assume someone else must already have checked it.
If our favorite preacher said it, we lower our guard.
If the message confirms something we desperately want to believe, sometimes we stop asking questions altogether.
But emotion cannot turn error into truth.
Popularity cannot turn error into truth.
Sincerity cannot turn error into truth.
A preacher's reputation cannot turn error into truth.
And even an unforgettable spiritual experience does not give us permission to rewrite what God has spoken.
That does not mean emotion is evil.
It means emotion is not the final authority.
The Bereans understood something the modern attention economy constantly tempts us to forget:
You can receive the Word eagerly without surrendering discernment.
Look carefully at Luke's description.
They “received the word with all readiness of mind.”
The Greek expression includes:
“μετὰ πάσης προθυμίας”
meta pasēs prothymias
With all eagerness. With readiness. With willing interest.
These were not cold-hearted cynics sitting in the back row waiting for Paul to make one mistake.
They wanted to hear.
They were receptive.
They were hungry.
But their hunger did not make them gullible.
They welcomed the message...
then examined the Scriptures.
That balance is beautiful.
An open heart.
An open Bible.
And perhaps some of us desperately need both again.
Because there is another extreme.
Some people distrust every preacher, every church, every teacher, every theological tradition, and eventually almost everyone except themselves.
That is not Berean discernment either.
The Bereans were not praised merely because they questioned.
They were praised because they tested what they heard against Scripture.
There is a difference between discernment and suspicion.
Suspicion says, “Nobody can tell me anything.”
Discernment says, “Show me what God has said.”
Suspicion makes the self the authority.
Biblical discernment submits the self—and the teacher—to God's Word.
That distinction matters.
Because you can escape one false teacher and still become captive to another authority:
yourself.
The Bereans did not replace Paul with personal preference.
They examined Paul's proclamation in light of Scripture.
And notice how often.
“Daily.”
καθ’ ἡμέραν.
Day by day.
Not only when something sounded suspicious.
Not only after a theological controversy exploded online.
Not only when someone sent them a video titled, “THIS PREACHER HAS BEEN EXPOSED.”
Daily.
Scripture was not merely their emergency fact-checking tool.
It was part of the rhythm by which they recognized truth.
And that may expose something in us.
When was the last time you checked?
Not your enemy's theology.
Yours.
Not the preacher you already dislike.
The preacher you love.
Not somebody else's assumptions.
Your assumptions.
Not merely the verses quoted in a sermon.
The verses you have repeated for years without ever reading what surrounds them.
Some of the most dangerous biblical misunderstandings are not necessarily blatant denials of Scripture.
Sometimes they are fragments of Scripture detached from their context and made to say more—or something different—than the inspired author intended.
That is why context matters.
Who is speaking?
To whom?
What comes before?
What comes afterward?
What kind of biblical literature are you reading?
Is this description or command?
Is this promise being addressed to a particular person or people in a particular covenantal setting?
How does this passage fit within the rest of Scripture?
And above all, how does our understanding fit the Gospel centered upon Jesus Christ?
Because biblical discernment is not about winning arguments.
It is about knowing Christ truly.
That is what makes the Berean story even more powerful.
Acts 17 does not describe Paul giving motivational advice.
Luke tells us what Paul had been doing immediately before arriving in Berea.
In Thessalonica, Paul went into the synagogue and for three Sabbaths reasoned with them from the Scriptures,
“Opening and alleging, that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead; and that this Jesus, whom I preach unto you, is Christ.”
Acts 17:3, KJV
There it is.
Jesus.
The suffering Messiah.
The risen Christ.
Paul was reasoning from Scripture that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and that Jesus is the Christ.
So when the Bereans searched the Scriptures, the question underneath their investigation was enormous:
Could this really be true?
Could the promised Messiah truly be the crucified Jesus?
Could the cross—an instrument associated with shame, suffering, and Roman execution—actually stand at the center of God's redemptive purpose?
Could apparent scandal become the doorway to grace?
And Scripture kept pointing them toward God's Messiah.
Then Acts says:
“Therefore many of them believed.”
Acts 17:12, KJV
Do not miss the order.
They heard.
They received.
They examined.
And many believed.
Biblical examination was not presented as the enemy of faith.
For many of them, examination accompanied the road toward faith.
Christianity does not ask you to believe that truth becomes dangerous when examined.
The Gospel can survive an open Bible.
Jesus does not need Scripture hidden in order to remain beautiful.
In fact, the more faithfully the biblical story is understood, the more staggering the Gospel becomes.
Because Scripture eventually forces us to confront a truth we would rather avoid.
Our greatest problem is not simply that other people have deceived us.
We have sinned.
The scandal is not merely out there.
It reaches into us.
The same Bible that helps expose false teaching also exposes the person holding the Bible.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23, KJV
That includes the preacher.
That includes the critic.
That includes the person in the pew.
That includes the person writing Christian posts.
That includes the person reading this one.
You.
Me.
All of us.
Scripture does not exist merely to give us ammunition against someone else's error.
It puts us on trial too.
It reaches behind the carefully managed Christian image.
Behind the worship playlist.
Behind the Bible verse in the bio.
Behind the church attendance.
Behind the theological vocabulary.
Behind the things nobody knows.
The resentment.
The secret compromise.
The pornography history you keep telling yourself you have under control.
The bitterness you have renamed “discernment.”
The pride disguised as doctrinal confidence.
The unforgiveness you can defend with an entire story.
The private messages you would never want projected onto the church wall.
The hunger for applause.
The jealousy.
The double life.
The prayerlessness.
The version of Christianity that wants Jesus as Savior but becomes uncomfortable when He speaks as Lord.
Scripture searches us while we search Scripture.
And suddenly the Berean question becomes personal.
“Are these things so?”
Is what I believe about Jesus actually what Scripture teaches?
Is what I believe about repentance actually biblical?
Is my definition of love biblical?
My definition of holiness?
My understanding of grace?
My understanding of salvation?
My understanding of myself?
Have I been following Jesus...
or a version of Jesus assembled from the parts of Christianity I find least offensive?
That question hurts.
But grace often enters through wounds truth was willing to uncover.
Jesus did not come merely to make religious people better at identifying everybody else's mistakes.
He came to save sinners.
He came for people whose lives have chapters they wish they could tear out.
People with scandal.
People with secrets.
People who knew better and still did it.
People who promised God, “Never again,” and found themselves crying over the same sin.
People who have been lied to.
People who have lied.
People wounded by churches.
People who wounded others while claiming to represent Christ.
People who are exhausted from pretending their faith is stronger than it feels.
And the answer of the Gospel is not, “Try harder until your past disappears.”
The answer is Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Lord.
The cross does not tell us sin was insignificant.
The cross shows us how serious sin is—and how astonishing God's grace is.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
And sinners are called to repent and believe the Gospel.
This is why testing teaching matters so much.
A distorted gospel can leave someone trusting in the wrong thing.
Their goodness.
Their religious performance.
Their money.
Their church membership.
Their favorite minister.
Their political tribe.
Their spiritual experiences.
Their ability to speak Christian language.
Their good deeds outweighing their bad ones.
But none of those things is Jesus.

Paul would later summarize the Gospel he had received and preached by pointing to Christ's death for our sins according to the Scriptures, His burial, His resurrection on the third day according to the Scriptures, and His appearances.
See 1 Corinthians 15:1–8.
According to the Scriptures.
There it is again.
The Christian faith is not supposed to float above the biblical text as an inspirational mist.
It has content.
It makes claims.
It announces what God has done in Jesus Christ.
And those claims matter eternally.
So please...
check this article too.
Do not believe something merely because Gospel Warrior published it.
Do not accept a Greek word merely because it looks impressive on a screen.
Open Acts 17.
Read verses 1 through 15.
Read the surrounding chapters.
Compare translations.
Use trustworthy lexical and historical resources when needed.
Read Scripture repeatedly.
Pray for wisdom.
Listen to mature believers and faithful teachers while remembering that every human teacher remains subordinate to God's Word.
And when somebody tells you, “The Bible says...”
develop the beautiful habit of asking:
Where?
Read it.
Then keep reading.
Because sometimes the verse really does say what you were told.
Sometimes it says something far richer.
And sometimes you will discover that a sentence you have heard repeated for fifteen years is nowhere in Scripture at all.
Do not panic when that happens.
Correcting what you believe because Scripture corrected you is not losing your faith.
It can be an act of faithfulness.
We should be willing to say:
“I was wrong.”
“I misunderstood that passage.”
“I repeated something I never checked.”
“I let a personality become too important.”
“I believed what I wanted to hear.”
“I used a verse outside its context.”
“I defended tradition before examining Scripture.”
“I need to learn.”
There is humility in those words.
And humility is desperately needed in an age where everybody can publish instantly and almost nobody is required to prove anything before thousands of people repeat it.
A thirty-second clip can travel around the world before somebody reads the chapter it quoted.
An emotional testimony can become doctrine.
A speculative interpretation can become “what the Bible clearly teaches.”
An invented quote can be placed over a picture of Jesus and shared hundreds of thousands of times.
And Christians can unintentionally participate in spreading things they never checked.
We can do better.
Not because we need to become arrogant Bible police.
Because truth matters.
Because people matter.
Because the reputation of Christ matters.
Because when we attach God's name to something God did not say, that is not a trivial matter.
And because there is a world full of hurting people trying to determine whether Christianity is true.
Some of them are watching how Christians handle truth.
So search the Scriptures.
Not to become impossible to teach.
Search so you become harder to deceive and easier for God's Word to correct.
Search until you stop needing every sermon to entertain you.
Search until a famous name cannot replace a faithful text.
Search until “but I feel...” no longer automatically ends the conversation.
Search until correction stops feeling like humiliation and begins feeling like mercy.
Search until you love truth more than the pleasure of being right.
And search until you realize that the center of Scripture is not your ability to search Scripture.
It is God's redemptive work fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
You can know Greek vocabulary and still need Jesus.
You can memorize entire books and still need Jesus.
You can detect theological errors and still need Jesus.
You can expose every false teacher on the internet and still stand before God as a sinner who needs mercy.
Discernment cannot atone for you.
Biblical knowledge cannot bleed for you.
Your doctrinal precision did not walk out of the tomb.
Jesus did.
That is where the road must lead.
From sin to repentance.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From death to life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps the person who most needs to hear this article is not somebody you know.
Perhaps it is you.
Maybe you have been spiritually living on other people's sermons for years.
Maybe your Bible stays closed while your Christian feed never stops scrolling.
Maybe you know what five influencers think about a verse but cannot remember the last time you sat alone with the passage.
Maybe you have been wounded by bad teaching and now distrust everyone.
Maybe you have followed a personality so closely that questioning his interpretation feels almost like questioning God.
Maybe you are not even sure what you believe anymore.
Then begin again.
Open the Bible.
Ask God for wisdom.
Read slowly.
Read honestly.
Look for Christ.
And do not be afraid of discovering that you need correction.
The God who corrects His children is not embarrassed by your need to learn.
And the Gospel is good news precisely because our hope was never supposed to rest upon our flawless understanding.
Our hope rests upon Christ.
Be honest.
Or comment, “I need to check the Scriptures,” if you have realized how easily you have accepted Christian-sounding claims without examining them.
And if you are exhausted, wounded, confused, or trying to rebuild your faith after spiritual deception, simply comment, “pray for me.”
There is no shame in needing prayer.
Someone reading your words may have been afraid to admit the same thing.
Even send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
Not because these words are Scripture.
They are not.
Save it so the next time a viral sermon, prophecy, theological claim, inspirational quote, or confident Christian voice lands on your screen, you remember what the Bereans did.
Then open the Bible.
Check.
Our desire is to keep placing Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and Gospel-centered nourishment in front of people who need Jesus.
You do not earn salvation by supporting a ministry. The grace of God cannot be bought. Salvation is God's gift in Christ.
Know Christ.
Read His Word.
Test what you hear.
Repent when Scripture exposes you.
Receive the grace Christ offers.
And refuse to build your eternal hope upon a human voice when God has given us His Word pointing us to His Son.
The Bereans checked Paul.
Surely we can check the internet.
Surely we can check our favorite preacher.
Surely we can check Gospel Warrior.
Surely we can check ourselves.
And when the Scriptures tear apart a comfortable lie, do not mourn the lie too long.
Because sometimes what feels like your faith falling apart is actually an assumption falling away...
and beyond it stands Jesus Christ, still true, still risen, still calling sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
Remember this when the next persuasive voice reaches your ears:
Never be so impressed by the person holding the Bible that you forget to open yours.
